newsitem.title: USA: Musicland seeks time and money - sources.
newsitem.headline: Musicland seeks time and money - sources.

text.p: Troubled Musicland Stores Corp has asked its vendors -- major record labels -- for concessions on payments while it seeks a much-needed infusion of third party cash, sources said.
"Musicland needs help and is in the process of reorganizing to get its financial house in order," said one executive from a record label seeking anonymity.
"We're working hard to improve our financial condition without filing Chapter 11," said a spokeswoman for Musicland, which hired Smith Barney in October to explore options.
"Unless something gives in the next few weeks, they could very well wind up filing for bankruptcy," said another executive from different record label.

The 750-store chain has asked distribution arms of Bertelsmann AG (BMG), Philips Electronics NV's Polygram, Sony Corp's Sony Music, EMI Group Plc, Seagram Co Ltd's Universal Records and Time Warner Inc's Warner Music to defer payments, with an option to convert the amounts due into equity in the company.
Sources said record labels were open to restating their payment packages, but not interested in an equity stake.

"The equity position plan was proposed, but I don't think it will be accepted. I think a variation of that plan, including a simple extension and spreading out of debt, will happen in the next week or two," said the label executive.
Sources said Musicland had $500 million in accounts payable due at December's end, although at least one vendor reported it had received payment in January.

"We don't have any bank payments due," said the Musicland spokeswoman, Beth Heming, who declined comment on the Big Six record companies, other than to say: "We do have very close contact with our vendors. We do work with them closely.
"Based on the terms that we have with our vendors right now, we're making all of our payments."
Furthermore, Musicland's revolving credit has consistently been at its upper limits, which has the record companies concerned it would face a cash-flow problem.
"Any plan's effectiveness will be contingent on Musicland renegotiating its revolving credit and/or bringing in an infusion of new money," said one record label executive.
Sources said Musicland has been talking with GE Capital and Apollo Advisors about possible cash infusions.
Sources also said some interested suitors have approached Musicland, which has closed 52 stores since December, but the company considered their bids as too low.
Heming would not comment on whether or not the company has received bids from suitors, or whether the company had talked to GE Capital and Apollo Advisers.

"There's no question that they're in trouble. You'd have to ask why would anybody want to buy into this industry right now," said Terrence McEvoy, analyst with Janney Montgomery Scott. "They've been stretching things out and trying to stay alive, but Chapter 11 might be one solution."
